mcq.q: Two fair dice are thrown. The probability that both dice show the same number is:
mcq.explain: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. Favourable outcomes (both dice show the same number): 6, e.g. (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4)…. Probability = 6/36 = 1/6. Counting only unordered pairs (21 of them) is wrong, because (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different outcomes.
mcq.fast: List favourable pairs on a 6 × 6 grid mentally; divide by 36.

mcq.q: Two fair dice are thrown. The probability that the product of the numbers is even is:
mcq.explain: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. Favourable outcomes (the product of the numbers is even): 27, e.g. (1, 2), (1, 4), (1, 6), (2, 1)…. Probability = 27/36 = 3/4. Counting only unordered pairs (21 of them) is wrong, because (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different outcomes.
mcq.fast: List favourable pairs on a 6 × 6 grid mentally; divide by 36.

mcq.q: Two fair dice are thrown. The probability that the numbers differ by exactly 4 is:
mcq.explain: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. Favourable outcomes (the numbers differ by exactly 4): 4, e.g. (1, 5), (2, 6), (5, 1), (6, 2). Probability = 4/36 = 1/9. Counting only unordered pairs (21 of them) is wrong, because (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different outcomes.
mcq.fast: List favourable pairs on a 6 × 6 grid mentally; divide by 36.

mcq.q: 3 fair coins are tossed together. The probability of getting exactly 2 heads is:
mcq.explain: Total outcomes = 2^3 = 8. Favourable outcomes (exactly 2 heads) = 3C2 = 3. Probability = 3/8 = 3/8. For "at least" questions the complement (1 − P(fewer)) is often quicker. Each coin has 2 equally likely faces, so all 2ⁿ outcomes are equally likely.
mcq.topic: Random experiments, sample space and events
mcq.fast: Use ⁿCₖ/2ⁿ for each count; use the complement for "at least one".

mcq.q: 4 fair coins are tossed together. The probability of getting at most 1 head is:
mcq.explain: Total outcomes = 2^4 = 16. Favourable outcomes (at most 1 heads) = 4C0 + 4C1 = 5. Probability = 5/16 = 5/16. For "at least" questions the complement (1 − P(fewer)) is often quicker. Each coin has 2 equally likely faces, so all 2ⁿ outcomes are equally likely.
mcq.topic: Random experiments, sample space and events
mcq.fast: Use ⁿCₖ/2ⁿ for each count; use the complement for "at least one".

mcq.q: One card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. The probability that it is a face card (jack, queen or king) is:
mcq.explain: Count favourable cards: 12 of 52. Probability = 12/52 = 3/13. A pack has 4 suits of 13 cards; hearts and diamonds are red; each suit has 3 face cards. Reduce the fraction to its lowest terms before matching the options.
mcq.fast: Count cards directly (avoid double counting the overlap), then reduce the fraction.

mcq.q: One card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. The probability that it is a red card or an ace is:
mcq.explain: Count favourable cards: 28 of 52. Add the two groups and subtract the cards that belong to both, so that no card is counted twice. Probability = 28/52 = 7/13. A pack has 4 suits of 13 cards; hearts and diamonds are red; each suit has 3 face cards. Reduce the fraction to its lowest terms before matching the options.
mcq.fast: Count cards directly (avoid double counting the overlap), then reduce the fraction.

mcq.q: One card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled pack of 52 cards. The probability that it is a red card or a 10 is:
mcq.explain: Count favourable cards: 28 of 52. Add the two groups and subtract the cards that belong to both, so that no card is counted twice. Probability = 28/52 = 7/13. A pack has 4 suits of 13 cards; hearts and diamonds are red; each suit has 3 face cards. Reduce the fraction to its lowest terms before matching the options.
mcq.fast: Count cards directly (avoid double counting the overlap), then reduce the fraction.

mcq.q: A bag contains 2 green and 2 yellow balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. The probability that one is green and the other yellow is:
mcq.explain: Number of ways to draw 2 balls from 4: 4C2 = 6. Favourable ways (one is green and the other yellow) = 2 × 2 = 4. Probability = 4/6 = 2/3. Using "with replacement" products (like (2/4)²) is wrong here because the first ball is not put back.
mcq.fast: Combinations: favourable selections ÷ ⁿC₂; or multiply conditional probabilities ball by ball.

mcq.q: A bag contains 3 green and 3 yellow balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. The probability that one is green and the other yellow is:
mcq.explain: Number of ways to draw 2 balls from 6: 6C2 = 15. Favourable ways (one is green and the other yellow) = 3 × 3 = 9. Probability = 9/15 = 3/5. Using "with replacement" products (like (3/6)²) is wrong here because the first ball is not put back.
mcq.fast: Combinations: favourable selections ÷ ⁿC₂; or multiply conditional probabilities ball by ball.

mcq.q: A bag contains 5 white and 7 black balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. The probability that one is white and the other black is:
mcq.explain: Number of ways to draw 2 balls from 12: 12C2 = 66. Favourable ways (one is white and the other black) = 5 × 7 = 35. Probability = 35/66 = 35/66. Using "with replacement" products (like (5/12)²) is wrong here because the first ball is not put back.
mcq.fast: Combinations: favourable selections ÷ ⁿC₂; or multiply conditional probabilities ball by ball.

mcq.q: P(A) = 0.2, P(B) = 0.6 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.1. Then P(A ∪ B) =
mcq.explain: Addition theorem: the chance of A or B equals the chance of A plus the chance of B minus the chance of both. With the given values, P(A ∪ B) = 0.2 + 0.6 − 0.1 = 0.7. Multiplying P(A) × P(B) is valid only for independent events.
mcq.fast: Write the addition theorem and solve for the unknown; use 1 − P(A ∪ B) for "neither".

mcq.q: P(A) = 0.2, P(B) = 0.2 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.1. Then P(A ∪ B) =
mcq.explain: Addition theorem: the chance of A or B equals the chance of A plus the chance of B minus the chance of both. With the given values, P(A ∪ B) = 0.2 + 0.2 − 0.1 = 0.3. Multiplying P(A) × P(B) is valid only for independent events.
mcq.fast: Write the addition theorem and solve for the unknown; use 1 − P(A ∪ B) for "neither".

mcq.q: P(A) = 0.2, P(B) = 0.7 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.1. The probability that neither A nor B occurs is:
mcq.explain: Addition theorem: the chance of A or B equals the chance of A plus the chance of B minus the chance of both. With the given values, P(A ∪ B) = 0.2 + 0.7 − 0.1 = 0.8. "Neither" is the complement of A ∪ B: 1 − 0.8 = 0.2. Multiplying P(A) × P(B) is valid only for independent events.
mcq.fast: Write the addition theorem and solve for the unknown; use 1 − P(A ∪ B) for "neither".

mcq.q: The probability that A solves the problem is 5/8 and that B solves it is 5/8, independently. The probability that exactly one of the two events happens is:
mcq.explain: For independent events, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 25/64. Exactly one = P(A)(1 − P(B)) + P(B)(1 − P(A)) = 15/32. Simply adding the probabilities double-counts the case when both happen, and can even give a value above 1.
mcq.fast: Work with complements: 1 − P(A), 1 − P(B); multiply for independence.

mcq.q: The probability that Ravi passes is 2/7 and that Sita passes is 2/3, independently. The probability that at least one of the two events happens is:
mcq.explain: For independent events, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 4/21. At least one = 1 − P(neither) = 1 − (1 − 2/7)(1 − 2/3) = 16/21. Simply adding the probabilities double-counts the case when both happen, and can even give a value above 1.
mcq.fast: Work with complements: 1 − P(A), 1 − P(B); multiply for independence.

mcq.q: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.7 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.4. Then P(B | A) =
mcq.explain: Conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) and P(B | A) = P(A ∩ B)/P(A). Here the condition is A, so divide 0.4 by 0.5: 4/5. Dividing by the wrong event is the classic slip.
mcq.fast: Divide the joint probability by the probability of the GIVEN event (after the bar).

mcq.explain: Conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) and P(B | A) = P(A ∩ B)/P(A). Here the condition is B, so divide 0.35 by 0.5: 7/10. Dividing by the wrong event is the classic slip.
mcq.fast: Divide the joint probability by the probability of the GIVEN event (after the bar).

mcq.q: The odds against an event are 1 : 4. The probability that the event happens is:
mcq.explain: Odds in favour a : b means a favourable cases for every b unfavourable, so P(happens) = a/(a + b). Odds against 1 : 4 means P(happens) = 4/(1 + 4) = 4/5. The ratio a/b itself is not a probability; a probability always compares favourable cases with ALL cases.
mcq.fast: Probability = (favourable part) ÷ (sum of both parts).

mcq.q: The odds in favour of an event are 1 : 7. The probability that the event happens is:
mcq.explain: Odds in favour a : b means a favourable cases for every b unfavourable, so P(happens) = a/(a + b). Here P = 1/8 = 1/8. The ratio a/b itself is not a probability; a probability always compares favourable cases with ALL cases.
mcq.fast: Probability = (favourable part) ÷ (sum of both parts).

mcq.q: A random variable X has the distribution P(X = 2) = 2/11, P(X = 4) = 5/11, P(X = 5) = 4/11. E(X) =
mcq.explain: E(X) = Σ x·P(x) = (2)(2/11) + (4)(5/11) + (5)(4/11) = 4. The simple average of the x-values (11/3) ignores the probabilities. E(X) is the long-run average value of X over many repetitions, so values with higher probability count more.
mcq.fast: Multiply each value by its probability and add (use a common denominator).

mcq.q: A random variable X has the distribution P(X = -3) = 5/11, P(X = 0) = 1/11, P(X = 5) = 4/11, P(X = 9) = 1/11. Var(X) =
mcq.explain: E(X) = 14/11 and E(X²) = Σ x²·P(x) = 226/11. Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² = 226/11 − 196/121 = 2290/121. Forgetting to subtract [E(X)]² gives E(X²). Variance measures how widely X spreads around its expected value and can never be negative.
mcq.fast: Var = E(X²) − [E(X)]²; build both sums in one pass.

mcq.q: A random variable X has the distribution P(X = -1) = 2/15, P(X = 2) = 2/5, P(X = 6) = 2/5, P(X = 9) = 1/15. Var(X) =
mcq.explain: E(X) = 11/3 and E(X²) = Σ x²·P(x) = 323/15. Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² = 323/15 − 121/9 = 364/45. Forgetting to subtract [E(X)]² gives E(X²). Variance measures how widely X spreads around its expected value and can never be negative.
mcq.fast: Var = E(X²) − [E(X)]²; build both sums in one pass.

mcq.q: A random variable X takes the values 1, 2, 3 with P(X = x) = kx. The value of k is:
mcq.explain: Probabilities of all values must add to 1: k(1 + 2 + 3) = 1, i.e. 6k = 1, so k = 1/6. Every probability is then between 0 and 1, as required for a valid probability distribution.
mcq.fast: k = 1 ÷ (sum of the values).

mcq.q: A random variable X takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 with P(X = x) = kx². The value of k is:
mcq.explain: Probabilities of all values must add to 1: k(1 + 4 + 9 + 16) = 1, i.e. 30k = 1, so k = 1/30. Every probability is then between 0 and 1, as required for a valid probability distribution.
mcq.fast: k = 1 ÷ (sum of the squares).

mcq.q: A number is chosen at random from 1 to 100. The probability that it is divisible by 7 or 11 is:
mcq.explain: Multiples of 7: 14; multiples of 11: 9; multiples of both (of LCM 77): 1. By the addition rule, favourable = 14 + 9 − 1 = 22. Probability = 22/100 = 11/50. Not subtracting the common multiples double-counts them.
mcq.fast: ⌊N/a⌋ + ⌊N/b⌋ − ⌊N/LCM⌋, then divide by N.

mcq.q: A number is chosen at random from 1 to 200. The probability that it is divisible by 6 or 5 is:
mcq.explain: Multiples of 6: 33; multiples of 5: 40; multiples of both (of LCM 30): 6. By the addition rule, favourable = 33 + 40 − 6 = 67. Probability = 67/200 = 67/200. Not subtracting the common multiples double-counts them.
mcq.fast: ⌊N/a⌋ + ⌊N/b⌋ − ⌊N/LCM⌋, then divide by N.

mcq.q: A committee of 4 is chosen at random from 5 men and 4 women. The probability that it has exactly 3 women is:
mcq.explain: Total selections = 9C4 = 126. Favourable = 4C3 × 5C1 = 4 × 5 = 20. Probability = 10/63. Remember to choose the men for the remaining 1 places as well; every committee of 4 is equally likely.
mcq.fast: (ways for women × ways for men) ÷ total ways — all combinations.

mcq.q: A committee of 3 is chosen at random from 5 men and 3 women. The probability that it has exactly 2 women is:
mcq.explain: Total selections = 8C3 = 56. Favourable = 3C2 × 5C1 = 3 × 5 = 15. Probability = 15/56. Remember to choose the men for the remaining 1 places as well; every committee of 3 is equally likely.
mcq.fast: (ways for women × ways for men) ÷ total ways — all combinations.

mcq.q: The probability that a randomly chosen non-leap year has 53 Mondays is:
mcq.explain: A non-leap year has 52 full weeks plus 1 extra day. The one extra day can be any of the 7 days, and only 1 of them is the given day. So the probability is 1/7.
mcq.topic: Random experiments, sample space and events
mcq.fast: Extra days beyond 52 weeks: 1 (ordinary) or 2 (leap); count how many of the 7 possibilities contain the day.

mcq.q: In a game a player throws a fair die. He wins ₹272 if the number is 5 or 6 and loses ₹90 otherwise. His expected gain per throw is:
mcq.explain: P(win) = 2/6 and P(lose) = 4/6. Expected gain = 272 × 2/6 − 90 × 4/6 = (544 − 360)/6 = ₹30.67. A positive value means the game favours the player in the long run.
mcq.fast: E = Σ (amount × probability), with losses negative.

mcq.q: In a game a player throws a fair die. He wins ₹83 if the number is 4, 5 or 6 and loses ₹32 otherwise. His expected gain per throw is:
mcq.explain: P(win) = 3/6 and P(lose) = 3/6. Expected gain = 83 × 3/6 − 32 × 3/6 = (249 − 96)/6 = ₹25.5. A positive value means the game favours the player in the long run.
mcq.fast: E = Σ (amount × probability), with losses negative.
